items.title: Peter Mandelson arrested in probe tied to Epstein

featured_image.name: UK police launch investigation into ex-envoy Mandelson over Epstein ties

items.description:
Peter Mandelson, the former UK ambassador to the United States, was arrested on Monday at his home in Camden, north London, on suspicion of misconduct in public office as part of a Metropolitan Police investigation into his ties to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.[1][2][3]

"Officers have arrested a 72-year-old man on suspicion of misconduct in public office. He was arrested at an address in Camden on Monday, 23 February and has been taken to a London police station for interview," the Metropolitan Police said in a statement. The arrest followed the execution of search warrants at two addresses in the Wiltshire and Camden areas.[3][4][1]

items.title: Ukraine marks 4 years of war with nearly 2 million casualties and no peace deal

featured_image.name: Ukraine updates: Kyiv marks 2 years since Russian invasion

items.description: As Ukraine prepares to mark the fourth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion on February 24, the war has exacted an almost incomprehensible human cost: nearly 1.8 million military casualties on both sides, more than 15,000 civilians killed, and millions displaced from their homes, with no peace agreement in sight.

items.title: Congo Basin lakes venting thousands-year-old carbon, study finds

featured_image.name: Peatland lakes in the Congo Basin release carbon that is ...

items.description: Two large blackwater lakes in the heart of the Congo Basin are acting as "chimneys," venting carbon that has been locked in surrounding peatlands for thousands of years, according to a study published Saturday in Nature Geoscience. The finding upends the long-held assumption that carbon stored in pristine tropical peat remains safely buried, and raises fresh concerns about the stability of one of the planet's most important carbon reservoirs.[1]

items.title: Russian small businesses buckle under wartime tax hikes as Ukraine invasion hits four years

featured_image.name: From bakeries to beauty shops, Russian businesses are feeling the ...

items.description:
As Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine marks its fourth anniversary, the economic toll of the war is reaching deeper into Russia's domestic economy. Small business owners across the country — from bakeries to beauty salons — report rising costs, collapsing demand, and a tax burden that has in some cases multiplied overnight, the result of sweeping fiscal reforms that took effect on January 1, 2026.

The reforms, signed into law by President Vladimir Putin in late November 2025, raised Russia's base value-added tax rate from 20% to 22% and drastically lowered the revenue threshold at which businesses must begin paying it — from 60 million rubles (approximately $783,000) to 20 million rubles ($261,000), with further reductions to 10 million rubles ($130,500) planned by 2028. The measures are designed to close a widening budget gap driven by soaring military expenditures and falling oil revenues.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Oil prices drop as US-Iran nuclear talks resume, tariffs rise

featured_image.name: Oil analysts say there is a supply glut — why that hasn't translated to lower prices this year

items.description:
Oil prices fell about 1% on Monday as the prospect of a third round of US-Iran nuclear talks eased fears of a military confrontation in the Middle East, while President Donald Trump's move to raise tariffs on all US imports to 15% added fresh uncertainty about the global economy.

Brent crude futures declined to around $71 a barrel, and US West Texas Intermediate futures dropped to roughly $66 a barrel, retreating after both benchmarks had surged more than 5% in the prior week on fears of a US-Iran military escalation.[1][2]

items.title: Ukraine marks four years since Russia's full-scale invasion amid fresh strikes

featured_image.name: Nationwide events mark fourth anniversary of Russia’s Ukraine invasion

items.description:
As February 24 arrives, marking the fourth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion, Ukraine and its global diaspora are pausing to mourn the dead, honor the displaced, and call on the world not to look away from Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II.

The anniversary comes days after Russia launched a massive combined missile and drone attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure. On February 22, the Ukrainian Air Force reported that Russia fired 50 missiles and 297 drones targeting power facilities in Kyiv, Odesa, and central Ukraine, killing at least one person in the capital and leaving six regions without electricity. President Volodymyr Zelensky said on X that in just one week, Russia had unleashed over 1,000 drones, more than 1,400 guided bombs, and 96 missiles. "Moscow continues to prioritize military actions over diplomatic efforts," he wrote.[1][2]

items.title: Stock futures slide as Trump raises global tariffs to 15%

featured_image.name: Tariff ruling live coverage: Trump attacks Supreme Court, imposes 10% 'global tariff', then raises it to 15%

items.description:
U.S. stock futures slipped on Sunday evening as investors weighed the fallout from a turbulent 48 hours in trade policy. President Donald Trump's decision to raise a new global tariff to 15% — the maximum allowed under the legal authority he invoked — rattled markets just two days after the Supreme Court struck down the bulk of his original tariff regime.

Dow Jones Industrial Average futures fell roughly 0.4%, while S&P 500 futures dropped about 0.5% and Nasdaq-100 futures declined approximately 0.7%, according to MarketWatch.[1][2]

items.title: Trump weighs broader Iran military action, including targeting Khamenei

featured_image.name: Iran says US risking ‘crisis’ as Trump sets ’10, 15 days’ deadline for deal

items.description:
President Donald Trump has told his advisers that if diplomatic efforts or an initial targeted strike fail to compel Iran to abandon its nuclear ambitions, he may authorize a broader military operation in the coming months — one that could include an attempt to remove Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei from power, according to the New York Times, citing individuals familiar with internal discussions.[1]

The revelation comes as U.S. and Iranian negotiators prepare to meet in Geneva on Thursday in what appears to be a last-ditch round of talks, with two aircraft carrier strike groups now positioned within striking distance of Iran.[2][1]

items.title: Pentagon presented Trump with plan to target Iran's Khamenei, reports say

featured_image.name: Trump says he's considering limited military strike against Iran

items.description:
President Donald Trump acknowledged on Friday that he is considering a limited military strike against Iran, even as the Pentagon has presented him with a range of scenarios that include options for targeting Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and his son Mojtaba, according to multiple reports citing senior administration officials.

"The most I can say — I am considering it," Trump told reporters at a White House breakfast with U.S. governors when asked about a potential limited strike if Iran fails to reach a deal over its nuclear program.[1][2][3]

items.title: Khamenei activates succession plan amid US strike threats, Times reports

featured_image.name: Ali Khamenei appoints succesor in event of US assassination

items.description:
The Pentagon has presented President Trump with military contingency plans that include a scenario to kill Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and his son Mojtaba, Axios reported Friday, a disclosure that has prompted Iran's top leader to activate emergency succession frameworks as the two nations edge closer to a potential armed confrontation.

"They have something for every scenario. One scenario takes out the ayatollah and his son and the mullahs," a senior Trump adviser told Axios, referring to Khamenei and Mojtaba, who is widely viewed as a likely successor. A second source confirmed the plan was floated to Trump several weeks ago. The adviser added: "What the president chooses no one knows. I don't think he knows."[1][2]

White House spokesperson Anna Kelly declined to discuss specific military plans, saying "only President Trump knows what actions he may or may not take."[2][1]

items.title: Oman confirms US-Iran nuclear talks set for Thursday in Geneva

featured_image.name: Iran's Araghchi arrives in Geneva for second round of nuclear talks with US

items.description:
The United States and Iran are preparing for a third round of indirect nuclear negotiations in Geneva this week, as both sides signal a willingness to keep talking even as President Donald Trump weighs military action against Tehran.

Oman's Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi confirmed on Sunday that the talks are scheduled for Thursday, describing the upcoming session as proceeding "with a positive push to go the extra mile towards finalising the deal." Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, appearing on CBS News' "Face the Nation" the same day, said he expects to meet US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff in Geneva on Thursday, adding, "I believe that still, there is a good chance to have a diplomatic solution which is based on a win-win game."[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Mexican army kills 'El Mencho,' leader of Jalisco cartel

featured_image.name: Leader of Mexico's Jalisco Cartel Reported Slain in Federal Raid

items.description:
The Mexican army killed Nemesio Rubén Oseguera Cervantes, the elusive leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel known as "El Mencho," during a military operation on Sunday in the western state of Jalisco, a federal official told the Associated Press. The death of one of the world's most wanted drug lords triggered a violent response from the cartel, with burning vehicles and roadblocks erupting across at least six Mexican states.[1][2]

The operation, carried out by special forces of the Mexican army and National Guard, took place in the mountainous area near Tapalpa in southern Jalisco, according to multiple Mexican media reports citing federal sources. El Mencho had long been reported to suffer from chronic kidney failure, which limited his mobility and forced him to rely on clandestine medical care in rural communities of Jalisco.[3][4][5][6]

items.title: Trump says US will send hospital ship to Greenland

featured_image.name: Hospital Ship USNS Comfort Departs on Humanitarian Mission

items.description:
President Donald Trump declared Saturday that the United States would send a "great hospital boat" to Greenland, claiming residents of the Arctic territory are "sick and not being taken care of." Denmark swiftly dismissed the plan, with the defense minister stating the self-governing territory's population already receives adequate healthcare.

Trump's announcement, made on Truth Social alongside an image of the USNS Mercy, a 1,000-bed naval hospital ship, came on the same day Danish military forces evacuated a crew member from a U.S. submarine off the coast of Greenland's capital, Nuuk, for urgent medical treatment. The timing raised questions about whether the submarine incident prompted the president's post.[1]

items.title: HKU engineers find physics principle that breaks sound absorption limits

featured_image.name: Unprecedented mechanical wave energy absorption observed in ...

items.description: Engineers at the University of Hong Kong have identified a physics principle that redefines the limits of noise reduction in ventilated spaces, offering a potential path toward quieter buildings, vehicles, and industrial environments without sacrificing airflow.

items.title: India postpones U.S. trade trip after Supreme Court strikes down Trump tariffs

featured_image.name: India delays Washington trade visit as U.S. policy shifts: source

items.description:
India has postponed a key trade delegation to Washington that was set to finalize an interim bilateral trade deal, after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down President Donald Trump's sweeping tariff regime and the White House scrambled to replace it with new levies under an untested legal authority.

The Indian negotiating team, led by chief negotiator Darpan Jain, had been scheduled to begin a three-day meeting in Washington on February 23 to convert a framework agreement into a binding legal pact, according to Reuters. Both governments agreed the visit should be rescheduled after they assess the fallout from Friday's court ruling and Trump's rapid imposition of replacement tariffs.[1][2]

"The visit of the Indian chief negotiator and delegation will be scheduled later at a mutually convenient date once both governments complete internal assessments," a source familiar with the matter told CNBC. A new date has not been set, though sources indicated to India Today that the delay is expected to last weeks rather than months.[3][4]

items.title: Two studies reveal Greenland ice is softer and melting faster than expected

featured_image.name: Scientists Find a 'Freak of Nature' Churning Deep in the Greenland Ice Sheet

items.description: Two new studies published this month have reshaped scientists' understanding of the Greenland ice sheet, revealing that it harbors slow, convection-like churning deep beneath its surface and that extreme melting events have intensified at an unprecedented pace since 1990. Together, the findings underscore how climate change is transforming the world's second-largest ice mass in ways researchers did not anticipate.

items.title: Greenland's ice sheet is churning like Earth's mantle, study finds

featured_image.name: ‘Freak of Nature’: Greenland Ice Sheet May Be Churning Like Molten Rock, New Models Show

items.description:
Giant plume-like structures deep inside the Greenland ice sheet, a mystery that has puzzled researchers for more than a decade, are likely caused by thermal convection — the same slow, churning process that moves molten rock in Earth's mantle, according to a study published this month in The Cryosphere.[1]

The finding, led by researchers at the University of Bergen in Norway alongside scientists from NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center and the University of Oxford, challenges the long-held view of ice sheets as rigid, static masses and could reshape how scientists model future sea level rise.[2][3]

items.title: France says EU ready to retaliate after Trump raises global tariff to 15%

featured_image.name: Trump to hike global tariffs to 15% from 10%, 'effective immediately'

items.description:
The European Union warned Saturday that it is prepared to strike back at the United States after President Donald Trump moved to reimpose and then escalate global tariffs in rapid succession, raising the prospect of a renewed transatlantic trade war less than 24 hours after the Supreme Court dealt a major blow to his trade agenda.

France's trade minister Nicolas Forissier told the Financial Times that Paris is coordinating with EU counterparts and the European Commission over Trump's decision to impose a blanket tariff on imports. "Should it become necessary, the EU has the appropriate instruments at its disposal," Forissier said. French officials told the newspaper that Brussels is weighing deployment of the anti-coercion instrument, a so-called "trade bazooka" that could restrict US technology companies from EU public procurement, impose export controls, or levy charges on services. A suspended package of retaliatory tariffs covering more than €90 billion in US goods could also be reactivated.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Scientists propose mission to chase interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS

featured_image.name: SPHEREx Captures Dramatic Outburst of Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS

items.description:
As interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS barrels toward a close flyby of Jupiter next month, scientists are both racing to study its surprising behavior and drafting plans for a spacecraft that could one day catch up to the alien visitor — even after it leaves the solar system for good.

The comet, only the third interstellar object ever detected, was discovered on July 1, 2025, by the NASA-funded ATLAS telescope in Chile. Since then, a fleet of space- and ground-based observatories has tracked it through the inner solar system. Now, as it heads outward past the orbit of Jupiter, new findings and a mission concept published this month have renewed scientific interest in the fleeting cosmic wanderer.[1]

items.title: Cuban security forces withdraw from Venezuela under US pressure

featured_image.name: Venezuela’s police, military pledge loyalty to interim President Rodriguez

items.description:
Cuban security advisers and medical personnel have been leaving Venezuela in recent weeks, marking a historic unraveling of the decades-old alliance between Caracas and Havana as Washington presses Interim President Delcy Rodríguez to sever ties with the island's communist government.

The withdrawals, first reported by Reuters on Saturday and confirmed by 11 sources familiar with the matter, represent the most concrete sign yet that the political bond holding together Latin America's two most prominent leftist governments is fraying under sustained American pressure.[1][2]
